subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pharmacology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: Pleuritic chest pain is best described as:

options.A: A dull, central, band-like pain radiating to the jaw
options.B: A severe, sharp, stabbing pain, worse on inspiration, and not reproduced by palpation
options.C: A burning retrosternal pain worse when lying flat or bending forward
options.D: Pain that is only ever felt during exercise and never at rest

questions.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, from inflammation of the parietal pleura, is classically a severe, sharp, stabbing pain that worsens on inspiration and is NOT reproduced by palpation — distinguishing it from musculoskeletal chest wall pain, which IS reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Despite his severe memory problems, patient H.M. had relatively normal short-term memory (e.g. could repeat six numbers forward after hearing them once) and intact memories from before his operation. What was specifically impaired?

options.A: His ability to form new long-term memories
options.B: His personality and IQ, both of which dropped sharply
options.C: His sense of touch and vision
options.D: His ability to speak or understand language

questions.explanation: H.M.'s deficit was specifically in forming new long-term memories (anterograde amnesia) — his immediate/short-term memory and his remote memories from before the surgery were largely preserved, illustrating that short-term and long-term memory, and the process of consolidating one into the other, are at least partly separable.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Memory Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: In hypospadias, why is ritual/routine circumcision specifically contraindicated in the newborn period?

options.A: Circumcision is never contraindicated in any condition
options.B: The foreskin is often needed later for the surgical reconstruction of the hypospadias
options.D: It has no bearing on hypospadias management at all

questions.explanation: In hypospadias, the deficient ventral foreskin tissue is often required for the surgical reconstruction of the urethra later on, so removing it via routine circumcision in infancy would compromise the corrective surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Hypospadias
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Which special test is specifically associated with assessing patellofemoral (patellar) instability?
questions.explanation: The apprehension test is used to assess for patellar instability — the examiner laterally displaces the patella and observes for a look or feeling of apprehension from the patient, who fears the patella is about to dislocate.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Allopurinol reduces uric acid production by acting as a competitive inhibitor of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol competitively inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to uric acid, which is why it is used to lower uric acid levels (e.g. in gout).
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Damage to Wernicke's area, located in the left temporal lobe, characteristically produces speech that is:

options.A: Completely absent — the patient cannot make any sound
options.B: Fluent in output but conveying little actual meaning, with impaired understanding of speech and written language
options.C: Slow and effortful but perfectly meaningful
options.D: Normal in every respect except pitch

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area damage markedly impairs comprehension of spoken and written language. Characteristically, the patient's own speech remains fluent in its flow and rhythm but conveys little coherent meaning.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Language Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: For a diagnosis of Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD), the symptoms of anxiety should have persisted for at least:
questions.explanation: Generalised Anxiety Disorder requires anxiety symptoms to have lasted for at least 6 months, with an insidious onset typically in the third decade and a stable, usually chronic course.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A fall on the outstretched hand causing tenderness in the anatomical snuff box most classically suggests a fracture of which carpal bone?
questions.explanation: Scaphoid fracture is common after a fall on the outstretched hand and classically presents with tenderness and swelling in the anatomical snuff box, plus pain on longitudinal percussion of the thumb and index finger.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SH) typically results from rupture of which type of vascular lesion?

options.A: A saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting large blood vessels
options.C: Atherosclerotic plaque in the carotid artery only
options.D: Venous thrombosis in the dural sinuses exclusively

questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically occurs from bleeding into the subarachnoid space, most often from rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting the larger cerebral blood vessels, often related to congenital weakness in the vessel wall.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Faradic-type currents are typically 'surged' for treatment purposes. What is the purpose of surging the current?

options.A: To reduce the total treatment time
options.B: To produce a near-normal tetanic-like contraction and relaxation of the muscle, by gradually increasing then decreasing the intensity of successive impulses
options.C: To eliminate the need for any electrodes
options.D: To convert the current into direct current permanently

questions.explanation: Surging gradually increases the intensity of successive impulses to a peak, then lets it fall (suddenly or gradually), mimicking a more natural, near-normal tetanic muscle contraction and relaxation cycle rather than an abrupt on/off stimulus.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Modified Faradic Currents
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Which historical event brought major attention to drug teratogenicity, resulting in thousands of infants born with phocomelia (seal-like limbs)?
questions.explanation: The thalidomide disaster (1958-61) resulted in thousands of babies born with phocomelia and other defects after the drug was used by pregnant women, and is the landmark event that focused medical attention on drug teratogenicity.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Teratogenicity
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Which of the following is described as a powerful, independent risk factor for stroke, associated with roughly a fivefold increase in risk?
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is described as a powerful risk factor for stroke, associated with approximately a fivefold increase in stroke risk, due to its potential to generate cardiac emboli.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: According to standard antenatal care guidance, the first antenatal visit should not be deferred beyond:
questions.explanation: The first antenatal visit should not be deferred beyond the second missed menstrual period — it may occur even earlier if the patient is considering termination of the pregnancy.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — Procedure at the First Visit
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Cataplexy, a feature of the classical narcolepsy tetrad, is characterised by:

options.A: Vivid dream-like hallucinations at sleep onset
options.B: A sudden loss of muscle tone (e.g. jaw drop or a fall), often precipitated by sudden emotion, with clear consciousness maintained
options.C: Complete loss of consciousness resembling a seizure
options.D: An inability to fall asleep at all

questions.explanation: Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone in various body parts (jaw drop, or paresis of skeletal muscles causing a fall), often precipitated by sudden emotion — importantly, consciousness remains clear and memory is normal during the episode (unless a sleep attack follows).
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Sleep Disorders — Narcolepsy
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Why is establishing a 1-RM (single maximum effort) considered inappropriate for certain patient populations, such as those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology?

options.A: It takes too long to administer in a clinical setting
options.B: It requires a single maximal effort, which carries risk for patients with joint impairments, healing soft tissue, osteoporosis, or cardiovascular pathology
options.C: It is only valid for measuring endurance, not strength
options.D: It cannot be performed using free weights

questions.explanation: A 1-RM test requires the patient to exert one true maximal effort, which is unsafe for patients with joint impairments, those recovering from or at risk of soft tissue injury, or those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology — alternative methods (e.g. multiple-RM formulas, dynamometry, percentage of body weight) are used instead for these patients.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Repetition Maximum, Precautions
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A BMI below which threshold is associated with significant hospital mortality risk?
questions.explanation: A BMI of less than 18.5 indicates nutritional impairment, but a BMI below 15 specifically is associated with significant hospital mortality risk.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Body Weight and Anthropometry
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A patient's gluteus medius is graded 4 (Good) on manual muscle testing. Which functional finding is consistent with this grade, per Daniels and Worthingham's discussion of why 'Good' is not always good enough?

options.A: Completely normal, symmetric gait with no compensation
options.B: A positive Trendelenburg sign during single-leg stance
options.C: Complete inability to abduct the hip against gravity
options.D: No palpable or visible muscle contraction at all

questions.explanation: Even a 'Good' (Grade 4) gluteus medius can be functionally inadequate — a positive Trendelenburg sign (contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance) can still appear, illustrating the gap between a manual muscle grade and real functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: What key feature distinguishes an obsession from a delusion?

options.A: An obsession is recognised as irrational and ego-alien, and the patient tries to resist it; a delusion is firmly believed and not resisted
options.B: A delusion always involves washing rituals while an obsession never does
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: An obsession is recognised by the patient as their own thought, but perceived as foreign (ego-alien), irrational, and something they try (unsuccessfully) to resist — insight is present. A delusion, by contrast, is a fixed false belief that the patient does not recognise as irrational and does not resist, because they genuinely believe it.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Definitions
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: The concept of a 'treatment threshold' in clinical decision-making primarily balances:

options.A: The doctor's personal preference against the hospital's budget
options.B: The risks of testing/waiting against the risks and benefits of starting treatment now
options.C: Only the cost of the test, with no consideration of patient risk
options.D: Nothing — treatment thresholds do not exist in evidence-based medicine

questions.explanation: The treatment threshold combines the risks of a test, and the risks versus benefits of treatment, to decide the point at which it makes sense to act. For a low-risk, effective intervention (e.g. antibiotics for a likely UTI), the threshold to act is lower; for a high-risk intervention, more diagnostic certainty is required first.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Dealing with Uncertainty
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: When one object partially blocks our view of another, we perceive the unobstructed object as nearer. This monocular depth cue is called:
questions.explanation: Interposition is the monocular cue where one object obstructing our view of another causes the fully visible object to be perceived as nearer, and the partially hidden object as farther away.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Sensory Processes and Perception — Monocular Cues for Depth Perception
questions.subject: Psychology
